questions.question: What happens when a Google Cloud project's spending exceeds a set budget threshold?
options: An alert is sent to warn administrators, but resources continue to run and spend.
Active resources are automatically paused until the billing cycle resets or is adjusted.
The linked billing account is suspended, preventing further charges from being incurred.
The project's API access is restricted to prevent any further resource deployment.
questions.answer: An alert is sent to warn administrators, but resources continue to run and spend.
questions.explanation: A budget alert is purely a warning mechanism. It does not automatically stop resources or cap spending.

questions.question: Why is it recommended to run applications on Cloud Run using built-in service accounts instead of using long-lived service account keys?
options: Cloud Run prevents workloads from using manual key files, meaning only automated credentials can be used.
Long-lived keys present a security risk if they leak, whereas Cloud Run can automatically retrieve short-lived credentials.
Service account keys expire after twenty-four hours, requiring constant manual updates from the development team.
Long-lived keys introduce network latency, whereas short-lived credentials allow for faster authentication times.
questions.answer: Long-lived keys present a security risk if they leak, whereas Cloud Run can automatically retrieve short-lived credentials.
questions.explanation: Long-lived keys are a security risk because they can leak. Cloud Run avoids this by automatically providing short-lived credentials to workloads.

questions.question: When deploying an update to an application running on Cloud Run, how are the changes managed?
options: The existing container is modified in place, updating only the specific files that have changed in the code.
A new unchangeable snapshot called a revision is created, allowing traffic to be shifted to it dynamically.
The application is temporarily taken offline while the container image is being overwritten by the system.
A new Google Cloud project is automatically generated to host the updated version of the container image.
questions.answer: A new unchangeable snapshot called a revision is created, allowing traffic to be shifted to it dynamically.
questions.explanation: Each deployment on Cloud Run creates a new revision, which is an unchangeable snapshot of the code and settings, and traffic can be moved between them.

questions.question: When using a Gemini model and requesting a response schema, why is validation of the model's output still necessary?
options: Structured output requires a manual decryption step before it can be read safely by the application.
A response that matches the requested structure perfectly can still contain incorrect information.
The model might return the output in a free-text format if it fails to interpret the requested schema.
The schema validation process automatically expires if it is not verified within a set time period.
questions.answer: A response that matches the requested structure perfectly can still contain incorrect information.
questions.explanation: Even if the output conforms perfectly to the requested schema shape, the information in the answer can still be incorrect.

questions.question: How does the Google Cloud resource hierarchy affect policy management?
options: Policies set at lower levels automatically override and erase policies set at higher levels.
Policies must be explicitly defined at the project level to take effect on resources.
Policies defined at higher levels of the hierarchy are automatically inherited by resources below.
Policies can only be applied to folders and cannot be applied directly to individual projects.
questions.answer: Policies defined at higher levels of the hierarchy are automatically inherited by resources below.
questions.explanation: The resource hierarchy is structured so that policies set at higher levels, such as the organisation or folders, are inherited by everything below them.
